messages.subject: name changes
parts:
I've always relied on relative.influence. After some faffing, I found
that it's now called relative_influence and it's arguments have
changed.

I think I'm happy to move to using summary directly to get at it, so
maybe it should be phased out and summary.GBMFit should get the
rescale and sort_it arguments.

In any event, if the name change to relative_influence is deliberate,
should we not have a function

relative.influence <- function(...){
message("relative.influence is deprecated. Use summary instead")
}

or something?

Given the too-ing and fro-ing of gbm.perf, I suspect it's not deliverate, though

On 12/08/2016 10:28 AM, Harry Southworth wrote:
> I've always relied on relative.influence. After some faffing, I found
> that it's now called relative_influence and it's arguments have
> changed.
>

I am going to jump on this. I pulled down the new code a couple weeks ago because a
project I'm working on really needs the id argument. (Long term study of cognition, and
subjects have multiple evaluations.) The model was badly overfitting, and this cured
that. A real home run.

But then, every gbm follow-up line in my established code broke. All of them. Every
single one. All the function names, all the arguments to the functions, the class of the
object, the components of that class --- there seems to have been a renaming spree. I
don't want to be too harsh, but this is simply insane. It is irresponsible to break
hundreds of lines of code (just here at my institution), and likely thousands of lines in
the world at large. At this stage I cannot recommend that our department ever install the
new version, simply from cost considerations.

How and when will this be addressed? It's on my todo list to create a careful test of the
survival code, but I'm not anxious to start given this issue.

My survival package is 20+ years old, and there are more than a few variable and/or
function names that would be different if I could go back in time. But if I tried to do
that now I'd have folks my lawn with pitchforks and torches, justifiably.

Terry Therneau

messages.subject: Re: name changes
parts:
Dependent packages are only a tiny part of the story (there are a dozen or so). The big
part is user code.

I am not talking about renaming, but UN-renaming. I'm guessing that a stack of sed
scripts and a couple days could undo the damage. This would be a small price to pay for
the pain the changes will cause. Just within our institution, creating a local gbm fork
would be less costly. Code and data for all our research studies is archived, and it is
not uncommon to need to reaccess it several years later. I have one project alone where I
could lose a week tracking down all the consquences of these.

A side discussion about our individual preferences for dot, underscore, and camel case
could be fun someday over a beer -- I could argue for or against any one of them if you
like. But in this case we are talking about serious pain and $ consequences; and for
what? So yes, I am pushing hard.

Terry Therneau

messages.author: 519907adbbc83e48
messages.subject: Re: name changes
parts:
There has been a fair amount of discussion about naming conventions in R. Perhaps before we (Paul/Harry) go about the business of un-renaming, we should hear what the design decision was.

When I first wrote gbm() the use of dots in function names was quite standard. But more recent style guides have pointed out that the dot was intended to signal the call of certain methods, like print.lm would call lm’s print method. But early R was a little careless and we have commonly used functions like read.table() that does not call a table’s read method. The over use of dots is now believed to be (perhaps) a little too sloppy. The old gbm naming conventions would not fit any of the current style guides (Wickham’s, Google’s, Paul Johnson’s).

If gbm were to move away from using dots it would join other packages (lme I think is an example) that went ahead and made the change. I worry that not updating the naming conventions would give gbm the look of an archaic package, like a lime green refrigerator (apologies if any of you still have a lime green refrigerator).

I’m with Terry that I have TONS of scripts written with relative.influence() and similar functions. Perhaps an in between version is to take Harry’s suggestion and create a relative.influence() function that calls relative_influence(), but also issues a warning that relative.influence() is deprecated.

Greg

Greg Ridgeway
Associate Professor
Department of Criminology
Department of Statistics
University of Pennsylvania

messages.author: c2082155b3674058
messages.subject: Re: name changes
parts:
On 12/09/2016 08:50 AM, Greg Ridgeway wrote:
> When I first wrote gbm() the use of dots in function names was quite standard. But more recent style guides have pointed out that the dot was intended to signal the call of certain methods, like print.lm would call lm’s print method.

I'll have to disagree here. The '.' in names was part of S many years before "print.lm"
and it's kindred appeared in the "Statistical Models in S" book (1993). I was used quite
commonly in variable names, though not much in base S function names --- the Bell folks
liked really short names --- but I see quite a few in my 1988 manual. Confusion arose
later when lots and lots of functions began to use methods, and it became the majority of
dots in function names. The recent change in R (recent in my timeline) to allow _ in
variable names prompted the big move away from dot, likely helped along by SAS converts.
So yes, non-dot function names are currently less confusing.

> But early R was a little careless and we have commonly used functions like read.table() that does not call a table’s read method. The over use of dots is now believed to be (perhaps) a little too sloppy. The old gbm naming conventions would not fit any of the current style guides (Wickham’s, Google’s, Paul Johnson’s).

I don't agree with everything Hadley says there, but it's mostly good. (e.g., my older
eyes prefer 4 space indentation rather than 2). I still use "." in a lot of variable
names, within a dataframe. It's a lot easier than underscore for this typist, which is
probably the main reason, but I actually kind of like it better anyway.

>
> If gbm were to move away from using dots it would join other packages (lme I think is an example) that went ahead and made the change. I worry that not updating the naming conventions would give gbm the look of an archaic package, like a lime green refrigerator (apologies if any of you still have a lime green refrigerator).

lme decided to move to S4 classes, which drives changes in a different way and has little
to do with dots, so I think that argument is a canard. (Suggest S4 for gbm if you want to
see me get really agitated. That's moving towards active persecution of the current
users.) The Hadleyverse changes names nearly as regularly as the seasons but I view that
as a case study against modification. And lime green appliances is a low blow: they were
ugly when when they were brand new.

I personally don't give a fig about the dated argument, see e.g. cox.zph in the survival
package. No, I wouldn't choose that name today. But then I'm dated myself, and simply
don't feel a need to dye my hair.

Let's see what we can do to minimise the pain.

For methods, can I suggest adding something like this:

If (missing(new_name) & !missing (old.name)) {
  message("stuff")
  new_name <- old.name
}

For functions

old.function <- function(old.name) {
  message(stuff)
  new_function(old.name)
}

Can someone make the necessary list; I have a few spare evenings?

Cheers,

pdm

On 12/09/2016 11:15 AM, Paul Metcalfe wrote:
Let's see what we can do to minimise the pain.

For methods, can I suggest adding something like this:

If (missing(new_name) & !missing (old.name)) {
  message("stuff")
  new_name <- old.name
}

For functions

old.function <- function(old.name) {
  message(stuff)
  new_function(old.name)
}

Can someone make the necessary list; I have a few spare evenings?

Cheers,

pdm

There is an argument for _ in function names due to the conflict with methods, but not a good one for argument names.  Secondly, the latter makes for long and clumsy .Rd files -- you have to document both you know.   I could live with old.function, under mild protest of course :-), but the old.name bit looks like more work up front as well as a long term documentation albatross. 

I'll find some time to look at the names: I'm gonna have to contribute something to balance out my griping...

Terry T.

parts:
old.name is pretty easy to document.

@param old.name see new_name

old.function is pretty easy too, with a similarly sparse documentation. So I don't think there's much burden there. Anyone who is actually reading it can follow the link, and I don't think it's a lot of work to do once we have the list.

I think this is really the best plan; it moves us towards a more modern R package that looks and feels like a modern R package, but also maintains, insofar as is possible, the old package API.

pdm

parts:
On 12/09/2016 12:32 PM, Paul Metcalfe wrote:
old.name is pretty easy to document.

@param old.name see new_name

old.function is pretty easy too, with a similarly sparse documentation. So I don't think there's much burden there. Anyone who is actually reading it can follow the link, and I don't think it's a lot of work to do once we have the list.

I think this is really the best plan; it moves us towards a more modern R package that looks and feels like a modern R package, but also maintains, insofar as is possible, the old package API.

pdm

Yes, Roxygen makes it fairly simple for you.  I'm thinking of the user, who parses a manual page that has lots of extra junk. It will not look the least bit more "modern" to have two spellings of a name than to have only the original.  Would anyone seriously suggest to R core that they do the same for read.table? 

Most certainly do not add nagware to the code in terms of warnings wrt parameter names.  That's just as fatal to the re-run of an old .Rnw report as outright failure.
